{{Short description|Rational mathematical function indexed by integer partitions}}
In mathematics, '''Weingarten functions''' are [[rational function]]s indexed by [[Integer partition|partitions of integers]] that can be used to calculate integrals of products of matrix coefficients over [[classical group]]s. They were first studied by {{harvtxt|Weingarten|1978}} who found their asymptotic behavior, and named by {{harvtxt|Collins|2003}}, who evaluated them explicitly for the [[unitary group]].

==Unitary groups==
Weingarten functions are used for evaluating integrals over the [[unitary group]] ''U''<sub>''d''</sub> 
of products of matrix coefficients.

Consider in general an integral of the form<math display="block">\int_{U_d} U_{i_1j_1}\cdots U_{i_nj_n}U^*_{i^\prime_1j^\prime_1}\cdots U^*_{i^\prime_{n'}j^\prime_{n'}}dU,</math>It can be shown that the integral would be zero, unless <math>n = n'</math>.<ref name=":0" /> Thus, consider only integrals of the form
<math display="block">\int_{U_d} U_{i_1j_1}\cdots U_{i_nj_n}U^*_{i^\prime_1j^\prime_1}\cdots U^*_{i^\prime_nj^\prime_n}dU,</math>
where <math>*</math> denotes complex conjugation. Note that <math>U^*_{ji}=(U^\dagger)_{ij}</math> where <math>U^\dagger</math> is the [[conjugate transpose]] of <math>U</math>, so one can interpret the above expression as being for the <math>i_1j_1\ldots i_nj_nj'_1i'_1\ldots j'_ni'_n</math> matrix element of <math>U\otimes\cdots\otimes U\otimes U^\dagger\otimes\cdots\otimes U^\dagger</math>.

This integral is equal to<math display="block">\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in S_n}\delta_{i_1i^\prime_{\sigma(1)}}\cdots\delta_{i_ni^\prime_{\sigma(n)}} \delta_{j_1j^\prime_{\tau(1)}}\cdots\delta_{j_nj^\prime_{\tau(n)}}W_{\sigma, \tau}(d)</math>where <math>W_{\sigma, \tau}(d) = \operatorname{Wg}(\sigma\tau^{-1},d)</math>, and <math>\operatorname{Wg}</math> is the '''Weingarten function''', given by
<math display="block">
\operatorname{Wg}(\sigma,d) = \frac{1}{n!^2}\sum_{\lambda}\frac{\chi^\lambda(1)^2\chi^\lambda(\sigma)}{s_{\lambda,d}(1)}
</math>
where the sum is over all partitions λ of ''n'' {{harv|Collins|2003}}. Here &chi;<sup>&lambda;</sup> is the character of ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> corresponding to the partition &lambda; and ''s'' is the [[Schur polynomial]] of &lambda;, so that ''s''<sub>&lambda;,''d''</sub>(1) is the dimension of the representation of ''U''<sub>''d''</sub> corresponding to λ.

The Weingarten functions are rational functions in ''d''. They can have poles for small values of ''d'', which cancel out in the formula above. There is an alternative inequivalent definition of Weingarten functions, where one only sums over partitions with at most ''d'' parts. This is no longer a rational function of ''d'', but is finite for all positive integers ''d''. The two sorts of Weingarten functions coincide for ''d'' larger than ''n'', and either can be used in the formula for the integral.

The integrals are called the '''link integrals''' in <math>U(N)</math> [[lattice gauge theory]].<ref name=":0" /> See <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Benoît |last2=Nechita |first2=Ion |date=2010-07-01 |title=Random Quantum Channels I: Graphical Calculus and the Bell State Phenomenon |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-010-1012-0 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=297 |issue=2 |pages=345–370 |doi=10.1007/s00220-010-1012-0 |arxiv=0905.2313 |bibcode=2010CMaPh.297..345C |issn=1432-0916}}</ref><ref>[https://ion.nechita.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Nechita-Tuebingen-Sep-2018.pdf Ion Nechita, "Weingarten calculus and applications to Quantum Information Theory" – Annual meeting of the SFB TRR 195 Tübingen – September 2018]</ref> for a graphical method for evaluating these integrals, inspired by [[String diagram|quantum string diagrams]].

=== Examples of Weingarten functions ===
The first few Weingarten functions<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Wg}(,d) &= 1\\
\operatorname{Wg}(1,d) &= \frac{1}{d}\\
\operatorname{Wg}(2,d) &= \frac{-1}{d(d^2-1)}\\
\operatorname{Wg}(1^2,d) &= \frac{1}{d^2-1}\\
\operatorname{Wg}(3,d) &= \frac{2}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}\\
\operatorname{Wg}(21,d) &= \frac{-1}{(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}\\
\operatorname{Wg}(1^3,d) &= \frac{d^2-2}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}\\
\operatorname{Wg}(4,d) &= \frac{-5}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-4)(d^2-9)} \\
\operatorname{Wg}(31,d) &= \frac{2d^2-3}{d^2(d^2-1)(d^2-4)(d^2-9)} \\
\operatorname{Wg}(2^2,d) &= \frac{d^2+6}{d^2(d^2-1)(d^2-4)(d^2-9)} \\
\operatorname{Wg}(21^2,d) &= \frac{-1}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-9)} \\
\operatorname{Wg}(1^4,d) &= \frac{d^4-8d^2+6}{d^2(d^2-1)(d^2-4)(d^2-9)}
\end{aligned} </math>
where permutations σ are denoted by their cycle shapes. For example, in <math>\operatorname{Wg}(,d) = 1</math>, the permutation is the trivial permutation on 0 elements. In <math>\operatorname{Wg}(21^2,d) = \frac{-1}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-9)} </math>, the permutation is the permutation on 4 elements that preserves 2 elements, and exchanges 2 elements.

There exist computer algebra programs to produce these expressions.<ref>Z. Puchała and J.A. Miszczak, [https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.4244 ''Symbolic integration with respect to the Haar measure on the unitary group in Mathematica.''], arXiv:1109.4244 (2011).</ref><ref>M. Fukuda, R. König, and I. Nechita, [https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.08539 ''RTNI - A symbolic integrator for Haar-random tensor networks.''], arXiv:1902.08539 (2019).</ref>

=== Examples of link integrals ===
<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\int_{U_d} dU U_{ij} \bar U_{k\ell}
&= \delta_{ik}\delta_{j\ell} \operatorname{Wg}(1,d) = \frac{\delta_{ik}\delta_{j\ell}}{d} \\
\int_{U_d} dU U_{ij} U_{k\ell} \bar U_{mn} \bar U_{pq}
&= (\delta_{im}\delta_{jn} \delta_{kp}\delta_{\ell q} + \delta_{ip}\delta_{jq} \delta_{km}\delta_{\ell n} ) \operatorname{Wg}(1^2,d) + (\delta_{im} \delta_{jq} \delta_{kp}\delta_{\ell n} + \delta_{ip} \delta_{jn} \delta_{km}\delta_{\ell q}) \operatorname{Wg}(2,d) \\
\int_{U_d} dU \; \overline{U_{11} U_{22} U_{33}} U_{12} U_{23} U_{31} 
&= \operatorname{Wg}(3,d) = \frac{2}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}
\end{aligned} </math>

===Asymptotics===
Given a permutation <math>\sigma</math>, there is a trivial part and a nontrivial part. The trivial part fixes elements, and the nontrivial part permutes the elements in cycles. This can be written out in the [[Permutation#Cycle notation|cycle notation for permutations]]. For example, the following permutation <math>(123)(45)(6)(7)(8)</math> has the nontrivial part <math>(123)(45)</math>.

Given a fixed permutation <math>\sigma</math> on <math>n</math> elements, as the size of the unitary group grows to <math>d \to \infty</math>, we have the [[Asymptotic analysis|asymptotic]] formula<math display="block">\operatorname{Wg}(\sigma,d) = d^{-n-|\sigma|}\left[\prod_{C_i \in \sigma}(-1)^{|C_i|-1}c_{|C_i|-1} +O(d^{-2})\right]</math>where <math>C_1, C_2, \dots</math> are the cycles of <math>\sigma</math>, <math>|C_i|</math> is the length of cycle <math>C_i</math>, <math>c_n := \frac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!}</math> is a [[Catalan number]], and <math>|\sigma|</math> is the smallest number of [[Transposition (mathematics)|transpositions]] (pairwise exchange) that <math>\sigma</math> is composed of. This formula can be used to prove that the algebra of the [[gaussian unitary ensemble]] converges to the [[Free probability|free probability algebra]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Benoit |last2=Matsumoto |first2=Sho |last3=Novak |first3=Jonathan |date=2022-05-01 |title=The Weingarten Calculus |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/202205/rnoti-p734.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=69 |issue=5 |pages=1 |doi=10.1090/noti2474  |doi-access=free|issn=0002-9920}}</ref>

Higher order expansions exist, of the form <math>d^{-n - |\sigma|}(a_0 + a_2 d^{-2}+ a_4 d^{-4} + \cdots)</math> where <math>a_0</math> is given above, and <math>a_2, a_4, \dots</math> are real numbers that depend on <math>\sigma</math> but not <math>d</math>. The full expansion is:<ref name=":0" /><math display="block">W_{\rho \sigma}(d)=\frac{(-1)^{\left|\rho^{-1} \sigma\right|}}{d^{n+\left|\rho^{-1} \sigma\right|}} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{\vec{W}_k(\rho, \sigma)}{d^{2 k}},</math>where <math>\vec{W}_k(\rho, \sigma)</math> is the number of '''weakly monotone walks''' on <math>S_n</math> from <math>\rho</math> to <math>\sigma</math> of length <math>\left|\rho^{-1} \sigma\right|+2 k</math>. To define weakly monotone walk, we construct the [[Cayley graph]] of <math>S_n</math>. Each directed edge is obtained by multiplying on the right by a [[Transposition (mathematics)|transposition]]. Now, a weakly monotone walk on the Cayley graph is a path <math>(i_1 j_1), (i_2 j_2), \dots</math> such that <math>j_1 \leq j_2 \leq \cdots</math>.

There exists a diagrammatic method<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Brouwer | first1=P. W. | last2=Beenakker | first2=C. W. J. | title=Diagrammatic method of integration over the unitary group, with applications to quantum transport in mesoscopic systems | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | date=1996 | volume=37 | issue=10 | pages=4904–4934 | doi=10.1063/1.531667 | arxiv=cond-mat/9604059 | bibcode=1996JMP....37.4904B }}</ref> to systematically calculate the integrals over the unitary group as a [[power series]] in ''1/d''.

=== Example asymptotics ===
Let <math>\sigma=(123)(45)(6)(7)(8)</math>. It acts on <math>n=8</math> elements. It decomposes into cycles with lengths <math>|C_1|=3</math>, <math>|C_2|=2</math>, <math>|C_3|=|C_4|=|C_5|=1</math>.

Applying <math>|\sigma|=n-k</math> with <math>k=5</math> cycles gives <math>|\sigma|=3</math>.

The Catalan factors are <math>c_{2}=2</math> for the 3-cycle, <math>c_{1}=1</math> for the 2-cycle, and <math>c_{0}=1</math> for each 1-cycle, so the product in the leading term equals <math>(-1)^{2}c_{2}\cdot(-1)^{1}c_{1}\cdot1^{3}=-2</math>.

Therefore the leading asymptotic term is <math>\operatorname{Wg}(\sigma,d)=-2d^{-11}+O(d^{-13})</math>.

Notice that in the above calculation, the trivial part <math>|C_3|=|C_4|=|C_5|=1</math> did not matter at all. This is because <math>(-1)^{|C_i|-1}c_{|C_i|-1} = 1</math> in that case. Thus in general, the asymptotic expression depends only on the nontrivial part of the permutation.

==Orthogonal and symplectic groups==
For [[orthogonal group|orthogonal]] and [[symplectic group]]s the Weingarten functions were evaluated by {{harvtxt|Collins|Śniady|2006}}. Their theory is similar to the case of the unitary group. They are parameterized by partitions such that all parts have even size.
